title: Redis: durability & replication
seriesDescription: How to use Redis in system design interviews: the data model, durability limits, clustering, caching, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, streams and pub/sub, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
description: RDB versus AOF, why acknowledged writes can vanish, asynchronous replication and why Redis is not a system of record.
source: Study notes: how to use Redis in system design interviews

questions.prompt: What do you lose if Redis crashes when it only uses RDB snapshots?

options.text: Everything written since the last snapshot.
options.why: Right: RDB is a periodic point-in-time copy.

options.text: Nothing, because every write is on disk before the reply.
options.why: That would require fsync on every write, which RDB does not do.

options.text: Only keys that have a TTL.
options.why: TTL has no bearing on what is persisted.

options.text: The keys but never the values.
options.why: Whole entries are lost, not parts of them.

questions.explanation: RDB trades safety for speed and a small footprint. Mention the window of loss explicitly.

questions.prompt: With AOF at its default, how much acknowledged data can a crash lose?

options.text: Up to about one second of writes, since it fsyncs once per second.
options.why: Right: the log is flushed each second by default.

options.text: Nothing at all, because every write is fsynced.
options.why: That needs the always setting, which few deployments use.

options.text: Everything since the last snapshot, which could be hours.
options.why: That describes RDB only.

options.text: Only writes made by clients that disconnected.
options.why: Connection state is not the issue.

questions.explanation: You can configure fsync on every write, but it costs the speed people chose Redis for.

questions.prompt: True or false: with its defaults, Redis gives the same commit-is-on-disk guarantee as a relational database.

options.text: True
options.why: It does not by default.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: defaults accept a window of loss.

questions.explanation: Redis intentionally trades that guarantee for speed. MemoryDB-style services give disk-based durability at some cost in latency.

questions.prompt: A primary acknowledges a write and dies before the replica sees it. The replica is promoted. What happened to the write?

options.text: It is lost, because Redis replication is asynchronous.
options.why: Right: the primary acknowledged before replicating.

options.text: It is recovered automatically from the client library cache.
options.why: Clients do not keep a durable copy of acknowledged writes.

options.text: It is replayed from the replica's own disk on promotion.
options.why: The replica never received it.

options.text: It stays pending and is applied when the old primary returns.
options.why: The old primary is replaced; its unreplicated writes are discarded.

questions.explanation: This is the deepest reason Redis is not a system of record, and it matters again for locks.

questions.prompt: You love Redis semantics but need disk-based durability. What is the interview-level answer?

options.text: Use a durable Redis-compatible service such as AWS MemoryDB, accepting some speed cost.
options.why: Right: durability is available if you trade a bit of speed.

options.text: Switch to RDB snapshots every second to make it durable for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Snapshots are periodic copies, not a per-write guarantee.

options.text: Add more replicas, since asynchronous replication is durable in a typical production setup.
options.why: Async replicas can still miss the last acknowledged writes.

options.text: Durability is impossible with any in-memory system.
options.why: Systems exist that journal writes durably.

questions.explanation: Or keep the system of record elsewhere and treat Redis as a fast layer in front of it.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about reading from Redis replicas.

options.text: In cluster mode, a client issues READONLY to allow reads from replicas.
options.why: Yes: otherwise it reads from primaries.

options.text: Replica reads can be stale by the replication lag.
options.why: Yes: that is the price of scaling reads.

options.text: Replicas multiply read capacity but not write capacity.
options.why: Yes: all writes still go to the primary of each slot.

options.text: Replica reads are always fully consistent with the primary.
options.why: No: replication is asynchronous.

questions.explanation: Replicas help reads and availability, not writes, and they do not make Redis a source of truth.

questions.prompt: A designer wants Redis as the only store for customer orders. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: Async replication and persistence loss windows mean acknowledged orders can vanish.
options.why: Right: that is unacceptable for a system of record.

options.text: Redis cannot store more than one value per key in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Values can be rich structures like hashes.

options.text: Redis has no way to look up an order by its key under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Key lookup is its strength.

options.text: Redis is too slow for order volumes.
options.why: Speed is not the problem.

questions.explanation: Keep orders in a durable database. Redis may cache them or hold derived data.
